findings.source_passage: the subtle insanity of Ahab respecting Moby Dick was noways more significantly manifested than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that
findings.why_it_matters: The phrasing 'subtle insanity of Ahab...noways more significantly manifested' is critically important — it encapsulates the paradox of Ahab's mad genius and is interpretively central; the draft reduces it to 'Ahab's subtle insanity showed in his shrewd sense,' losing the rhetorical precision and the 'noways more significantly manifested' formulation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'the subtle insanity of Ahab respecting Moby Dick was noways more significantly manifested than in his superlative sense and shrewdness' verbatim or very close to it.

findings.source_passage: The permanent constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence — 'the permanent constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness' — is one of the chapter's most quotable and interpretively charged formulations, encapsulating Ahab's political philosophy; the draft drops the embedded 'thought Ahab' and the precise 'manufactured man' framing into a compressed clause that obscures the free-indirect voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the sentence verbatim: 'The permanent constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness.'

findings.source_passage: In times of strong emotion mankind disdain all base considerations; but such times are evanescent.
findings.why_it_matters: This antithetical sentence sets up the entire Crusader analogy and the cash passage; the draft collapses it into 'strong-emotion disdain is evanescent,' losing the rhetorical structure (the generalization about mankind, the adversative 'but') that gives the argument its satirical weight.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full antithesis: 'In times of strong emotion mankind disdain all base considerations; but such times are evanescent.'

findings.source_passage: and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew if so disposed, and to that end competent, could refuse all further obedience to him
findings.why_it_matters: The qualification 'both moral and legal' and the careful 'if so disposed, and to that end competent' carry the legal-rhetorical register that distinguishes Melville's prose here; the draft simplifies to 'with impunity the crew might refuse obedience,' losing those nuances.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain 'with perfect impunity, both moral and legal' and 'if so disposed, and to that end competent' to preserve the register.

summary: No high-severity signature losses; three medium-severity voice-flattening failures weaken the chapter's most interpretively charged formulations (the 'manufactured man' sentence, 'noways more significantly manifested,' and the 'strong emotion/evanescent' antithesis), but the draft's overall fidelity — including full preservation of the 'cash…cashier Ahab' passage and the tools/moon line — keeps it just below the regeneration threshold.
